quote: I got a question. Where is it you calling?
stewart_read: Customer is questioning the legitimacy/source of the call. The schema calls for honest specificity to reduce suspicion. Rep's first response ('I'm sorry. From from Ion Solar.') stumbles and only on the second attempt references the form.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have simply misheard the question rather than failed the protocol, since she does recover by 00:55 with the form reference.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to lead with the form-reference specificity immediately on any 'who is this' question rather than repeating the company name alone — specificity is what resolves suspicion, not just naming the company twice.

quote: Before, somebody was come to see that, but, I was, pay something for the tenant, like, rent or something, the rental.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a prior solar-adjacent visit that involved a rental/tenant payment structure — potentially a lease or third-party financing pitch. Rep does not probe what company this was or what was offered.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged the disclosure too garbled/unclear to be worth probing given the customer's language barrier and the call's time pressure.
coaching_implication: Even a single follow-up ('was that a lease, and do you remember the company?') would give the closer competitive context on what the customer was previously pitched and rejected.

quote: I'm disability now, and I can I don't I'm not working, so I can pay? Okay.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a disability status and inability to work, directly bearing on her ability to take on any new payment. Rep's next line pivots straight to homeowner confirmation without acknowledging the disclosure.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be strategically deferring the emotional response to focus on qualification first, planning to circle back once ownership is confirmed.
coaching_implication: This is a trust-gift disclosure per schema; the rep should acknowledge it directly before continuing the qualifier sequence, not file it and move to the next checkbox.

quote: Yeah. I am own home, but I don't know. I need to talk my child when I
stewart_read: Customer signals her adult child is a co-decision-maker, the same structural pattern as spouse-on-title protocol. Rep responds 'For sure' and immediately pivots back into the savings pitch without ever circling back to identify or include the child.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep's 'For sure' could be read as an acknowledgment intended to be revisited at booking, but no appointment was ever booked, so the co-decision-maker was never captured or confirmed.
coaching_implication: This is the same schema violation as excluding a spouse — the co-decision-maker must be named and included on any appointment. Coach the rep to ask 'what's your child's name, and can they be on the call with us?' immediately when this surfaces.

quote: So you still pay for the solar panels, but it's less than what you're paying ComEd right now.
stewart_read: This is the rep's one direct, honest answer to the customer's repeated affordability question — a partial credit against the broader pattern of scripted deflection. But it's still a feature-level explanation, not a flip that reframes the ComEd bill itself as the villain costing her money regardless of solar.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as adequate transparency rather than a missed flip, since the rep does answer the question honestly rather than dodging it.
coaching_implication: Credit the rep for directness here, but note the missed inversion — the sharper move ties her fixed income directly to 'what you can't afford is paying ComEd every month with no way to lower it,' not just a comparative statement.

quote: I can't pay nothing because all my all my manager, Social Security give it to me is for the mortgage.
stewart_read: Second, more specific disclosure of fixed income entirely consumed by mortgage. Rep's response at 03:26 ('Right. So are you paying your electric bills?') moves straight into another verify question rather than acknowledging the severity of what was just shared.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be trying to get to the actual bill payer (the daughter) to keep the qualification moving, which is a legitimate procedural need.
coaching_implication: The procedural need is real, but a one-line acknowledgment ('I hear you — I want to make sure this actually works for your situation') costs nothing and preserves trust before the next qualifier question.

quote: So we do require a credit score above 670. Is that the case for you, or is it lower than 670?
stewart_read: Rep runs the standard credit qualifier on a customer who has disclosed disability income, no discretionary funds, and dependency on a daughter for bill help — a profile very unlikely to clear underwriting even if the credit score is technically above 670.
alternative_hypothesis: Procedurally correct per script — the setter's job is to ask, not to pre-judge affordability, so continuing the qualifier is defensible.
coaching_implication: This is schema-correct procedure, but the manager should discuss whether the floor wants setters to flag likely non-viable financial profiles for a supervisor check before pushing a full appointment cycle, given the customer's disclosed circumstances.

quote: Let me check, and I talked to my daughter. She she can check. I'll let you know. I can call you back.
stewart_read: Call ends with the customer, not the rep, owning the next step. No day/time, no locked callback window, no text-confirmation promise.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the customer's stated need to check her credit score and consult her daughter, a hard booking attempt here would have been premature — deferring may be the only honest path forward.
coaching_implication: Even when a hard book isn't appropriate, the rep should lock a specific callback window ('I'll check back with you Thursday afternoon — does that work?') rather than leaving it fully open-ended.
